questions.q: Define 'warp' and 'weft' yarns in a woven fabric. State the direction of each relative to the selvedge.
questions.a: Warp yarns run parallel to the selvedge (lengthwise/grain line); weft yarns run perpendicular to the selvedge (crosswise). A wrong answer (e.g., swapping directions, saying both run parallel) reveals the student cannot visualise the loom's geometry — they memorise terms without understanding the physical setup where warp is held under tension and weft is inserted across.

questions.q: A fabric shows a clear diagonal rib running at 45° on the face. The interlacing repeats every 3 warp and 3 weft threads (over 2, under 1). Identify the weave type and its notation. Explain why this weave is stronger than plain weave for the same yarn and sett.
questions.a: It is a 2/1 twill (warp-faced), notation: ↑↑↓ (or 2 up, 1 down). Twill has fewer interlacings per repeat (3 vs 2 in plain), allowing yarns to pack more closely → higher thread density → more yarns per unit area share the load. A wrong answer citing "more interlacings = stronger" reveals the misconception that interlacing frequency alone determines strength, ignoring yarn packing and crimp.

questions.q: Draw the draft (threading plan), peg plan (lifting plan), and interlacing diagram for a 5-end satin weave (warp-faced) using straight draft on 5 shafts. Show one complete repeat.
questions.a: Draft: 1-2-3-4-5 (straight). Peg plan (lifting order for warp-faced satin): shaft 1 up, 2 up, 3 up, 4 up, 5 down (or cyclic permutation: 1,2,3,4,5 with one shaft down per pick). Interlacing: each warp floats over 4 wefts, under 1; staggered so no two adjacent warps have the down at same pick. A wrong answer with random lifting order or missing the 'move number' concept (e.g., 2 for 5-end) reveals the student doesn't grasp the mathematical rule: satin requires a move number (s) coprime to repeat size (n), where s ≠ 1, n-1.

questions.q: Compare handloom and modern air-jet loom on: (a) primary motions mechanism, (b) maximum picks per minute, (c) suitability for fancy weaves. Present as a 3×2 table.
questions.a:
| Feature | Handloom | Air-jet Loom |
|---------|----------|--------------|
| Shedding | Treadle/lever (manual) | Cam/dobby/electronic (automated) |
| Picking | Shuttle (hand-thrown) | Compressed air jet (shuttleless) |
| Beating | Hand-operated sley/reed | Crank/connecting rod (mechanical) |
| Max ppm | 40–60 | 800–1500+ |
| Fancy weaves | Limited (dobby possible) | Excellent (electronic jacquay/dobby) |
A wrong answer claiming handloom has higher ppm or air-jet uses shuttle reveals confusion between traditional and modern technology categories.

questions.q: A designer wants a fabric with high lustre, smooth surface, and good drape for evening wear, but it must resist snagging better than traditional satin. Evaluate: 5-end satin vs 8-end satin vs sateen (weft-faced satin). Recommend one with justification.
questions.a: Recommend **8-end sateen (weft-faced)**. Reasoning: (1) Longer floats (7/1) than 5-end (4/1) → higher lustre; (2) Weft-faced means floats are on surface but weft yarns can be finer/more numerous → smoother; (3) Sateen structure (weft floats) distributes stress better than warp-faced satin when snagged — a pulled weft float relieves locally without distorting warp tension. 5-end satin has shorter floats (less lustre) and warp-faced structure snags more visibly. A wrong answer choosing 5-end satin for "more interlacings = stronger" misses that snag resistance depends on float behaviour, not interlacing count.

questions.q: Design a derivative weave by combining plain and 2/2 twill in a check pattern: 8 ends plain, 8 ends 2/2 twill, repeat. Draw the draft for 16 shafts (straight draw) and write the lifting sequence for the first 8 picks. Explain how the fabric will behave differently at the transition zones.
questions.a: Draft: Shafts 1–8 = plain (alternating 1,2,1,2...), Shafts 9–16 = 2/2 twill (straight 9,10,11,12,13,14,15,16). Lifting (first 8 picks, plain area): Pick 1: shafts 1,3,5,7 up; Pick 2: 2,4,6,8 up; repeat. Twill area lifting (2/2): Pick 1: 9,10 up; Pick 2: 10,11 up; Pick 3: 11,12 up; Pick 4: 12,13 up; Pick 5: 13,14 up; Pick 6: 14,15 up; Pick 7: 15,16 up; Pick 8: 16,9 up. Transition zones: plain-to-twill boundary creates a line of differing crimp and float length → potential puckering or weft distortion; requires careful tension balancing. A poor answer ignores transition effects or gives random lifting, showing inability to plan multi-weave structures.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Woven fabric is a textile structure formed by interlacing two sets of yarns — warp (______) and weft (crosswise) — at right angles to each other on a loom, following a specific interlacing pattern called a weave.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're holding a cotton shirt and a denim jean — both are woven, but one is smooth and light, the other is ______-ribbed and heavy.
What is Woven fabric? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Woven fabric is a textile structure formed by interlacing two sets of yarns — warp (lengthwise) and weft (crosswise) — at right angles to each other on a loom, following a specific interlacing pattern called a weave.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to: (1) identify and label the main parts of a handloom and power loom from a diagram, (2) draw the draft, peg plan, and interlacing diagram for plain, twill (2/1, 2/2, 3/1), and satin (5-end, 8-end) weaves, and (3) explain how weave structure influences fabric properties (strength, drape, lustre, durability).
